outline.section: H2: What Is SLS and Why Is It in Toothpaste?
outline.guidance: Explain what sodium lauryl sulfate is: a surfactant (foaming agent) used in toothpaste primarily to create lather and help distribute the paste across teeth. Clarify that SLS is the ingredient responsible for the foamy feel most people associate with brushing. Note that SLS is also found in shampoos, body washes, and dish soap — helping readers connect the ingredient to a broader 'clean personal care' context that aligns with Real Skin Care's brand. Explain why manufacturers use it: it is inexpensive, effective as a surfactant, and has a long safety history in low-concentration rinse-off products. Do NOT exaggerate risks. Be balanced. Then transition: despite its widespread use, a meaningful segment of people experience sensitivity, canker sores, or oral irritation that may be linked to SLS exposure. CITATION REQUIREMENT: The writer must cite at least one credible source on SLS and oral mucosal sensitivity. Suggested source for researcher to confirm: Herlofson BB and Barkvoll P (1994), 'Sodium lauryl sulfate and recurrent aphthous ulcers,' Acta Odontologica Scandinavica — this is a frequently referenced study in dentistry literature. The writer should verify this citation is accessible and accurate before including it; do not fabricate or paraphrase beyond what the source supports.

outline.guidance: This section expands the audience beyond people who already know they want SLS-free — it speaks to people who are researching whether they need to make the switch. Cover three audiences explicitly: (1) People with recurring canker sores or mouth ulcers — note the possible connection to SLS (cite the same study referenced above or a supporting source); (2) People with sensitive gums or oral tissue; (3) People on a broader clean-beauty or natural personal care journey who want to eliminate synthetic surfactants across all products. Keep language inclusive and non-diagnostic — do not tell readers they have a medical condition. Use phrases like 'if you notice...' and 'many people find...' Tie back to the brand's core value: Real Skin Care exists for people who read labels. This section should feel like helpful triage, not a scare tactic.

outline.section: H2: How to Read a Toothpaste Label: What 'SLS-Free' Actually Means
outline.guidance: This is a high-value educational section that no current top-10 result covers adequately — make it genuinely useful. Explain that 'SLS-free' means sodium lauryl sulfate is not listed in the ingredients. However, alert readers to related compounds that may appear in its place: SLES (sodium lauryl ether sulfate / sodium laureth sulfate) and SCS (sodium coco sulfate). Clarify that these are distinct chemicals with different irritation profiles — SLES is generally considered milder; SCS is a coconut-derived surfactant sometimes marketed as 'natural' but is still a sulfate. Explain that a truly clean, gentle toothpaste may use alternative surfactants like cocamidopropyl betaine (milder, often coconut-derived) or no surfactant at all. Remind readers that 'SLS-free' alone does not make a toothpaste natural or clean — they should also look at other ingredient categories (artificial sweeteners, synthetic dyes, parabens). Include a brief 3-item label-reading checklist in this section (formatted as a short bullet list) to improve scannability. This section builds brand authority as a trustworthy ingredient educator.

outline.section: H2: SLS-Free vs. Fluoride-Free: Do You Need Both?
outline.guidance: Many readers searching for SLS-free toothpaste are also interested in fluoride-free options — these two preferences often travel together in the natural oral care audience. This section briefly explains the distinction: SLS-free refers to the absence of a foaming surfactant; fluoride-free refers to the absence of a specific active ingredient with its own debate. Clarify that a toothpaste can be SLS-free but still contain fluoride, or both SLS-free and fluoride-free. Do not take a strong editorial stance on fluoride for or against — instead, note that different people have different preferences based on their oral health needs and values, and that Real Skin Care offers options across both categories. outline.section: H2: Frequently Asked Questions About SLS-Free Toothpaste
outline.guidance: Include 5 FAQ items formatted with H3 subheadings for each question. These should target real downstream queries visible in Reddit and dentist-review content currently ranking. Suggested questions: (1) 'Does SLS-free toothpaste still foam?' — Answer: some do (using alternative surfactants like cocamidopropyl betaine), some produce minimal foam; foaming is cosmetic and not required for effective cleaning. (2) 'Is SLS-free toothpaste better for canker sores?' — Answer: some people report fewer and less severe canker sores after switching; reference the cited study from earlier in the post. (3) 'Is SLS-free toothpaste safe for kids?' — Answer: generally yes, and children with sensitive mouths may particularly benefit; recommend checking with a pediatric dentist for specific guidance. (4) 'Can I use SLS-free toothpaste if I have sensitive teeth?' — Answer: SLS-free formulas are often recommended for sensitive mouths; look for formulas with gentle abrasives and soothing ingredients. (5) 'What is the difference between SLS-free and sulfate-free toothpaste?' — Answer: explain that SLS is one sulfate; sulfate-free is the broader category excluding SLS, SLES, and other sulfate surfactants. Write answers in a conversational, confident tone — not overly clinical. Each answer should be 2-4 sentences.
